title: Factory, builder, and object composition patterns
hook: JavaScript favors plain objects and factory functions over deep class hierarchies. Factories hide validation; builders assemble complex configs; composition replaces inheritance without nominal type ceremony.

blocks.text: A **factory function** returns a configured object or closure — `createUser()`, `makeLogger(level)`. A **builder** accumulates steps fluently before `build()` — useful for HTTP clients, test fixtures, and query DSLs. **Object composition** merges behaviors with spread, Object.assign, or small mixin functions instead of subclassing. In JS these patterns enforce **invariants at creation** (validation, defaults, private state via closure) because there is no constructor overload syntax like C#.

entries.plainDefinition: Function that returns new objects without new keyword — central JS idiom.
entries.example: function createPoint(x, y) { return Object.freeze({ x, y }); }

entries.plainDefinition: Stepwise API chaining setters until build produces immutable result.
Combine small modules instead of extending a base class.
Immediately invoked function exposes public API, hides private vars.
entries.example: export const counter = (() => { let n = 0; return { inc() { n++; } }; })();

blocks.text: React hooks, Express middleware stacks, and fetch wrappers all use factories and composition. Misusing `class extends` in JS creates fragile prototype chains and `this` binding bugs. Senior code centralizes **defaults, validation, and telemetry** in factories so call sites stay one line. C# uses constructors + DI; JS uses factory + module scope + optional DI containers (Inversify, tsyringe).

blocks.title: Interview trap: class versus factory
blocks.body: Prefer factory + closure when you need private state without #fields. Prefer class when instanceof semantics or framework requires it (React.Component legacy). Justify tradeoff.

blocks.title: Pitfalls to avoid
blocks.body: Shallow-cloning shared default objects. Exporting mutable singletons callers mutate. Builder without build() validation. Deep class hierarchies where composition would be clearer.

blocks.text: Production: factories are the seam for **testing** — inject fake clock, stub fetch, swap Redis. Document required options in TS types; validate in factory for runtime. For libraries, prefer `createX(config)` over global mutable config. Builders should fail fast in build(), not half-constructed states.

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Defaulting to class inheritance for every problem. Not mentioning shallow copy of defaults bug. Cannot compare to C# DI and explain where validation lives in JS stack.

interviewTakeaways: JS idiomatic construction: factory functions, options objects, composition over inheritance.
Validate and normalize in one factory — not at every call site.
Clone nested defaults — shallow spread shares mutable arrays/objects.
60s: Factories hide validation and private closure state. Builders for many optional fields. C# uses ctor+DI; JS uses createFn at module boundary. Watch shared DEFAULTS bug.
Follow-up: design createPaymentClient with retries, timeout, and test doubles.
commonPitfalls: Shared mutable default object mutated by one instance affecting all others.
Class hierarchies where mixins or composition would reduce coupling.
Strong answer: factory validates, freezes or clones, C# DI parallel, builder for complex configs.
